short: Everything conditioned changes and passes away.
beginner: Anitya means impermanent. Everything we experience — bodies, feelings, thoughts, situations — changes. Seeing this clearly is a key step in many Indian paths.
what: Anitya (Pali anicca) is impermanence. In Buddhism it is one of the three marks of existence, with dukkha and anatta: whatever is conditioned arises and passes away, and clinging to it brings suffering. Hindu traditions also stress the impermanence of the body and world, but usually contrast it with a permanent reality (the Self or Brahman), which Buddhism does not posit. The Gita repeatedly calls the world transient and advises enduring passing experiences.
scholar: Abhidharma and later Buddhist logicians (such as Dharmakirti) developed the doctrine of momentariness (kshanikavada): real things exist only for a moment. Nyaya and Mimamsa argued against momentariness, defending enduring substances and selves. In Vedanta the nitya/anitya viveka (discrimination between permanent and impermanent) is the first of the qualifications of the seeker.

perspectives.view: Impermanence is a mark of all conditioned phenomena; insight into it undermines craving and the sense of a lasting self.
Advaita teaches discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal: the world and body are impermanent, while the Self is permanent and unchanging.
Nyaya accepts that composite things are impermanent but argues against Buddhist momentariness, defending enduring atoms, substances and selves.
Jain thought holds that substances are permanent while their modes change, applying its many-sided method to permanence and change.
The Guru Granth Sahib frequently reminds the listener of the passing nature of the world and wealth, contrasting it with the eternal Name.

follow.note: Contacts giving heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go; endure them.
The unreal has no being and the real never ceases: the Gita's contrast of changing and unchanging.
